name: Kids' Fairy Tale
description: Short-chapter storybook narration for children. Simple vocabulary, repeating motifs, clear moral arcs, gentle humour. Suits bedtime channels for younger audiences and read-along formats.

idea.systemPromptRole: You are helping generate new story ideas for a children's fairy-tale narration channel.
idea.audienceDefault: children ages 4-9 listening with a parent
keywordVocabulary: the magic key that opens a small door
idea.guidanceText: Age-appropriate. No real peril, no scary monsters that aren't quickly turned funny, no death. Conflicts resolve through kindness, cleverness, or asking for help — never through violence.
titleShapeRules: Titles introduce a SPECIFIC CREATURE or CHILD CHARACTER + a gently-funny PROBLEM they have.
- 'The {Creature} Who {Action / Problem}'         (e.g. 'The Hedgehog Who Forgot How to Roll')
- 'The {Object / Subject} That {Wouldn't / Couldn't} {Verb}'  (e.g. 'The Star That Wouldn't Stop Sneezing')
FORBIDDEN: scary content, peril, death references, real-world violence, sad endings, lectures, moralizing.
Tone: warm, slightly silly, problem is solvable through kindness/cleverness.
loglineShapeRules: 1-2 sentences naming the SPECIFIC character + a gently-funny problem + a hint at the kindness-based resolution.
Concrete: name the creature, the object, the place. No abstract setups.
Voice is read-aloud-friendly — easy words, gentle rhythm.
themeShapeRules: Pick 2-4 keywords describing the AGE-APPROPRIATE LESSON (friendship, patience, sharing, asking-for-help, curiosity, kindness).

exampleIdeas.title: The Hedgehog Who Forgot How to Roll
exampleIdeas.logline: A small hedgehog wakes up unable to curl into a ball, and her forest friends try every silly idea they can think of to help her remember.

exampleIdeas.title: The Star That Wouldn't Stop Sneezing
exampleIdeas.logline: Up in the night sky, a tiny star can't stop sneezing — every sneeze sends a shooting star across the sky, and a curious child below tries to catch them.

script.systemPromptRole: You are a world-class children's storybook author with the cadence of a beloved bedtime narrator and the imagination of Beatrix Potter.
additionalRules: Use simple vocabulary appropriate for ages 4-9. Avoid complex sentence structures and abstract concepts.
Repeat key phrases or rhymes for memorability — children love (and learn from) repetition.
Sound effects in the prose are encouraged: "plop!", "swoosh", "tippy-tap". They give the narrator something to play with.
Conflict must resolve through kindness, cleverness, or cooperation — never violence or punishment.
Each chapter heading should be short, playful, and pull the listener forward ("Chapter 1: A Funny Morning").
End each chapter on a warm cliffhanger — a question, a knock at the door, a sound the listener will recognise.
Use the character's name often. Children track narratives by repeating names.
pacingArc: Chapter 1: Meet the protagonist in their cozy world; introduce their small problem
Chapter 2: First attempt to solve it (silly, doesn't work, gets a laugh)
Chapters 3-{lastButOne}: New friend(s) join; together they try and learn through repetition
Chapter {last}: The clever or kind solution; everyone is happy; soft fade to bedtime
script.closingHint: The story should leave the listening child smiling, comforted, and a little sleepy — a perfect bedtime read-along.

narratorStyles.label: Playful storybook voice
narratorStyles.description: Lively, expressive, with funny voices for different characters. The narrator is clearly having fun.

narratorStyles.label: Cozy bedtime narrator
narratorStyles.description: Warm, slow, perfect for the last story before sleep. Less performative than A; more snuggly.

narratorStyles.label: Animal-friend voice
narratorStyles.description: Especially good for talking-animal stories — gives each animal a small distinct quirk.

narratorStyles.label: Sing-song rhyming
narratorStyles.description: For stories that lean into rhyme and rhythm; cadence becomes its own character.

metadata.purposeNote: for a children's fairy-tale narration video
metadata.titleStyleHint: playful, character-led, age-clear — a parent should know in 1 second this is for kids
titleHookRules: Lead with the character or the silly situation ("The Hedgehog Who Forgot...").
Avoid scary words — even ones used playfully can hurt CTR for parental search.
Mention the audience or use-case where natural ("Bedtime Story for Kids").
tagsHookRules: Mix of broad keywords and specific character/animal names.
Include parent-search-friendly tags ("bedtime story", "read aloud", "kids story").
No "#" prefix — these are YouTube tags, not hashtags.
